name: Netaji Jayanti at Giddapahar
image_query: Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose museum Kurseong
summary: Every 23 January, Subhas Chandra Bose's birth anniversary, Kurseong remembers him at the Giddapahar house where the British held him under house arrest in 1936. Expect flag-hoisting, school groups, songs and speeches at the museum.
body: Subhas Chandra Bose was born on 23 January 1897, and the date is marked across India; the national government has called it Parakram Diwas since 2021. In Kurseong the day has a particular meaning, because the house on Giddapahar is one of the few places in the hills tied directly to his life. His brother Sarat Chandra Bose bought it in 1922, and Netaji was confined there under British house arrest in 1936.

On the morning of the anniversary, the museum and the local community hold a commemoration: the flag is raised, garlands are laid at his portrait or bust, students from Kurseong's schools sing and recite, and local officials and residents speak. The house is busier than on any other day of the year.

It is not a festival in the sense of fairs and food stalls; it is a day of remembrance. For travellers, it is a chance to see the museum full of local people and to understand how strongly Kurseong holds on to this part of its story.
tips: Arrive by 9 am; the main programme is usually in the morning.
Dress modestly and keep photography respectful during the ceremony.
Combine with Eagle's Crag on the walk down, as the morning air in January is usually clear.

faqs.q: What happens at Giddapahar on Netaji Jayanti?
faqs.a: A morning commemoration at the Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Museum: flag-hoisting, garlanding of his portrait or bust, songs and recitations by schoolchildren, and short speeches. Local residents and officials attend. It is a day of remembrance rather than a fair, and the museum is busier than usual.

faqs.q: Why is Netaji remembered in Kurseong?
faqs.a: His elder brother Sarat Chandra Bose bought the Giddapahar house in 1922, and Netaji stayed there several times. In 1936 the British held him there under house arrest for several months, and he wrote many letters from the house. It is now a museum.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend the Netaji Jayanti programme?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors usually join respectfully as part of the crowd. Keep to the back, follow any instructions from organisers and avoid using flash during the ceremony. Check current status before you travel, as the programme and museum hours can change.

faqs.q: How cold is Kurseong on 23 January?
faqs.a: Typically about 5–13 °C, with clear, dry mornings and cold evenings. Wear a warm jacket, especially on the exposed Giddapahar hill. January mornings often give good views over the plains from the museum garden and Eagle's Crag.

name: Dashain and Tihar in Kurseong
when: Sept–Nov, by the Hindu lunar calendar (Dashain first, Tihar about three weeks later)
summary: The two biggest festivals of the Nepali-speaking hills. Dashain brings red tika and blessings from elders; Tihar, about three weeks later, brings oil lamps, garlands for crows, dogs and cows, rangoli and the sel roti of every kitchen.
body: Dashain is the longest and most important festival for Nepali-speaking Hindus, celebrated over about two weeks at the same time as Durga Puja in Bengal. Its high point is the day of tika, when elders place a mixture of red vermilion, yoghurt and rice on the foreheads of younger relatives and give blessings and a little money. Families travel home, new clothes come out, and in villages tall bamboo swings, called ping, are sometimes put up.

Tihar follows about three weeks later, at the same time as Diwali. Over five days, crows, dogs and cows are honoured in turn with garlands and tika, houses are lit with oil lamps and fairy lights, and groups of young people go from house to house singing bhailo and deusi songs for small gifts. Kitchens fry sel roti, a ring-shaped rice bread, in large batches.
In Kurseong you see it in the bazaar, which fills with marigold garlands and new clothes, and in the lights on the hillsides at night.
tips: Book transport early; Dashain and Puja are the busiest travel period of the year.
Accept sel roti if a host offers it, and ask how it is made.
Some shops and offices close on the main days, so carry cash and plan meals.

faqs.q: When are Dashain and Tihar celebrated?
faqs.a: Dashain falls in September or October and lasts about two weeks, at the same time as Durga Puja. Tihar comes about three weeks later, in October or November, at the same time as Diwali. Exact dates follow the lunar calendar and change each year; check current status before you travel.

On the main day of Dashain, elders place a paste of red vermilion, yoghurt and rice on the foreheads of younger family members, often with barley shoots called jamara, and give blessings. It is the heart of the festival, and families gather for it.

Sel roti is a ring-shaped bread made from a rice-flour batter, sweetened and deep-fried. It is made in large batches for Tihar and Dashain and shared with neighbours and visitors. It is slightly crisp outside and soft inside, and is often eaten with tea or potato curry.

faqs.q: Is it a good time to visit Kurseong during Dashain and Tihar?
faqs.a: Yes for atmosphere: lights, marigolds, songs and festive food. But it is also the busiest travel time, coinciding with Durga Puja and Diwali holidays from the plains. Book rooms and jeeps early and expect higher prices.

name: Losar at Bokar Monastery
image_query: Losar Tibetan New Year monastery prayers
summary: Tibetan New Year at the Kagyu monastery above Mirik. Monks hold special prayers in the days around Losar, prayer flags are renewed and Buddhist families from the area come up in their best clothes to make offerings.
body: Losar is the Tibetan New Year, celebrated by Tibetan Buddhists and by many Buddhist communities across the Himalaya. It falls in February or March, depending on the Tibetan lunar calendar. Before it comes a period of cleaning and of rituals to clear away the obstacles of the old year; on and after New Year's Day come prayers, offerings, visits to family and new prayer flags on the rooftops and ridges.

At Bokar Monastery, founded above Mirik by Bokar Rinpoche in 1984, the monks hold special prayers around the New Year, and Buddhist families from Mirik and the surrounding tea villages come up in traditional dress to light butter lamps, make offerings and receive blessings. Programmes vary year to year.
For visitors it is a calm, colourful time to see the monastery as a living community. Keep to the edges, dress modestly and follow the monks' lead.
tips: Ask at the monastery a few days ahead for the year's programme.
Walk clockwise around the prayer wheels and the monastery.
Do not photograph monks or rituals inside the prayer hall without permission.

faqs.q: When is Losar at Bokar Monastery?
faqs.a: Losar follows the Tibetan lunar calendar and usually falls in February or March. The exact date changes every year. Check the date for the year and ask the monastery about its programme before you travel, as ceremonies vary.

faqs.q: Can visitors attend Losar prayers at Bokar?
faqs.a: Usually yes, quietly and respectfully. Dress modestly, remove shoes where asked, sit at the back and do not photograph inside the prayer hall without permission. Some rituals may be private to the monastic community.

faqs.q: Is there a mask dance at Bokar for Losar?
faqs.a: We have not confirmed a regular cham mask dance at Bokar for Losar, so do not plan on one. Ask the monastery for the year's programme. Prayers, offerings and family visits are the core of the celebration.

faqs.q: What should I bring to the monastery at Losar?
faqs.a: Nothing is required. Many visitors offer a white khata scarf or a small donation, and some bring butter-lamp offerings. Bring warm clothes, as February mornings in Mirik are cool, and a little cash for the donation box.

name: Sittong Orange Festival
summary: A December celebration of the orange harvest in Darjeeling's orange village, which the West Bengal Directorate of Cinchona and Other Medicinal Plants has organised. Expect fruit stalls, local food and cultural programmes in the Riyang valley.
body: Sittong lives on the Darjeeling mandarin, and December is when the orchards are at their best. The Directorate of Cinchona and Other Medicinal Plants, the state body that runs the cinchona plantations in this area, has organised an orange festival at Sittong in December to showcase the harvest and bring visitors to the village.

When it is held, the festival brings stalls of oranges and orange products, local food, and cultural programmes with songs and dances from the hill communities. It is a small, village-scale event rather than a big fair.

Dates and whether it takes place in a given year are announced locally, so ask a Sittong homestay or check current status before you travel. Even without the festival, December in Sittong is orange season, and every house has fruit.
tips: Confirm the festival dates with a Sittong homestay before booking.
Book rooms early; December is Sittong's busiest month.
Buy oranges directly from growers rather than resellers.

faqs.q: Is the Sittong Orange Festival held every year?
faqs.a: It has been organised in December by the Directorate of Cinchona and Other Medicinal Plants, but we cannot confirm it happens every year or on fixed dates. Ask a Sittong homestay or local contact and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens at the Sittong Orange Festival?
faqs.a: When held, it features stalls selling oranges and orange products, local food and cultural programmes such as songs and dances. It is a modest village festival, not a large commercial fair, and it celebrates the orange harvest that Sittong is known for.

faqs.q: Is December a good time to visit Sittong even without the festival?
faqs.a: Yes. December is the peak of orange season, with fruit on the trees and on sale at every house, and the weather is usually dry and clear. Nights are cold, so bring warm clothes and ask for extra blankets.

faqs.q: How much do oranges cost in Sittong?
faqs.a: In season, buying directly from growers, expect roughly ₹60–120 a kg depending on size and the year's harvest. Prices are usually lower than in Siliguri markets. Bulk buyers pay by the basket.
